ground_truth_core_content:
Introduction:
**0:** Both sections recap prior lessons and transition into multimodal data, then explain why it matters and preview the lesson; these functions are present. However, the expected section illustrates text-only limitations with three specific examples (financial reports, medical documents, building sketches), and the generated section retains only one of the three (financial reports), substituting 'technical diagrams' and a vague 'other visual documents' catch-all for the other two. Dropping two of three named GT examples is the majority of a short, specific list, not a single item inside a longer interchangeable one, so this is treated as a genuine content gap rather than trivial compression.

Limitations of Traditional Document Processing:
**1:** Both sections cover the same core argument (normalizing to text loses information), the same 5-step OCR/layout-detection pipeline, and the same rigid/fragile/slow-costly characterization with cascading errors. The generated section substitutes an '88-94% baseline accuracy' statistic for the expected section's general 'performance ceiling' framing -- an addition, not an omission.

Foundations of Multimodal LLMs:
**1:** Unlike a previous generation for this same episode, this section now includes the text-tokenization/image-patching analogy, the contrastive-learning alignment mechanism, and named image-encoder examples (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP) -- all present in the expected section and previously a gap in this preset. The named current-model list is partial (Llama 4 and GPT-5 only, vs. the expected section's seven names spanning both open- and closed-source), but it still preserves the core open-source-vs-closed-source dichotomy the expected section draws, so this is treated as acceptable compression rather than a missing idea. The one idea still absent is the expected section's closing paragraph on extending the architecture to other modalities like audio or video via additional encoders -- a single remaining gap, flagged as borderline below given how much of the rest of the section is now covered.

Applying Multimodal LLMs to Images and PDFs:
**1:** Unlike a previous generation for this same episode, this section now demonstrates all seven conceptual steps: raw bytes, Base64, public URL, private GCS URL (previously missing), object detection, and -- shown with actual code this time rather than a one-line dismissal -- PDF as bytes and Base64. The final PDF-object-detection step is reduced to a single descriptive sentence with no code, but the concept itself is present, which is enough to preserve the section's core content.

Foundations of Multimodal RAG:
**0:** The generic ingestion/retrieval architecture, ColPali's OCR-bypassing role, the bag-of-embeddings representation, and the late-interaction/MaxSim query mechanism are all present. However, unlike a previous generation of this same episode, this version never names the PaliGemma-3B/SigLIP backbone that the expected section uses to identify what ColPali actually is -- this is a specific, named technical fact (the model's own identity), not a decorative statistic, and its total absence is treated the same way the missing named-encoder-examples were treated in the Foundations of Multimodal LLMs section. This is flagged as borderline below since it involves the same style of judgment call as that section.

Implementing Multimodal RAG for Images, PDFs, and Text:
**0:** The mini-project framing, the image-description workaround (again naming Voyage and Cohere), and the indexing/search pseudocode are present, and -- unlike a previous generation of this section -- the transformer-architecture query demonstrating PDF-page retrieval is now included. However, this version drops the complementary kitten/robot query that demonstrates standard-image retrieval within this section; that example only resurfaces later as the agent's test question in the following section, not as a RAG-retrieval demonstration here. Since the section's stated scope is 'Images, PDFs, and Text,' running only one of the two within-section demonstrations is the same category of gap as the reverse omission scored in a previous generation, just affecting the complementary half.

Building Multimodal AI Agents:
**0:** The tool definition, agent-building code (with the correct note that LangGraph is covered in Part 2), test question, and final answer are all present, and this version explicitly recaps the combined skills (structured outputs, tools, ReAct, RAG), which is a nice callback. However, the expected section opens by explicitly naming the two general ways multimodality can be added to agents (multimodal inputs, or specialized multimodal tools) before narrowing to the RAG-tool example; the generated section skips this framing entirely and jumps straight into integrating the specific RAG tool. This taxonomy is a distinct idea from the specific implementation that follows it, and its total absence is why this scores 0 despite the section otherwise being solid.

Conclusion:
**1:** Both sections wrap up Part 1 and transition to the Part 2 capstone. The expected section recaps the specific combined techniques (structured outputs, tools, ReAct, RAG) before transitioning; this generated section instead recaps the OCR-to-native-processing shift. As with a previous generation of this section, this is treated as an acceptable variation in wrap-up framing rather than a missing idea, since both serve the same function and the capstone preview itself closely mirrors the expected section's own description.

References:
**1:** Both sections contain a numbered list of references serving the same bibliographic purpose.
